# Data understanding {#sec-data}

*Measurements below are tagged with where they can be reproduced: **EDA §n** means section n of the
exploratory notebook, **FE §n** section n of the feature-engineering notebook; both are named in the
reproducibility note that closes this section.*

## The dataset and the unit of observation

We use the Columbia speed-dating experiment of @fisman2006gender: 21 events, called *waves*, run
between 2002 and 2004. Within a wave every participant met each opposite-sex participant for a
four-minute date and then privately recorded whether they would like to see that person again. The
published file holds 8,378 rows over 195 columns and describes 551 participants (EDA §2).

One row is a **directed encounter** — participant `iid` meeting partner `pid`, recorded from `iid`'s
point of view — so every meeting appears twice, once from each side. We verified this mirror
structure rather than assuming it: for all 8,368 rows carrying a partner identifier the mirrored row
is present, the partner's own decision equals the `dec_o` field stored on our row on 100% of rows,
and `match` equals the conjunction of the two decisions on every row (EDA §3, FE §4).
The ten rows without a partner identifier were dropped, as no pairwise feature is defined for them.
Each participant appears in exactly one wave and no date crosses a wave boundary, which is what
makes the wave a clean unit for cross-validation (@sec-protocol).

| Property | Value | Property | Value |
|:-------------------------|:-----------|:--------------------------|:-----------|
| Rows × columns | 8,378 × 195 | Participants per wave | 10–44 (med. 24) |
| Participants / waves | 551 / 21 | Partners per participant | 5–22 (med. 16) |
| Directed encounters used | 8,368 | Acceptance rate (`dec`) | 42.0% |
| Mirrored rows present | 8,368 of 8,368 | Mutual match rate | 16.5% |

: The dataset at a glance; values from EDA §3–§6 and FE §4. {#tbl-data-summary}

Feedback is **implicit and binary**, and we retain both readings of it: the directional `dec`
records one person's decision and is the natural training target, while the symmetric `match`, true
only when both parties accept, is the relevance label for ranking. Matches are far rarer than
acceptances — 16.5% against 42.0% — so the positive class is small and accuracy would be a
misleading measure (EDA §5). Acceptance is also markedly gendered, and the distinction between
*giving* and *receiving* matters: men accepted 47.4% of the partners they met and women 36.5%, which
seen from the receiving end means women were accepted 47.9% of the time and men 37.2% (EDA §5 and
§9). A model blind to the decider's gender is therefore miscalibrated for one of the two groups.

## Candidate sets, and whether the data can be evaluated

![Left: participants per wave, i.e. the 21 cross-validation folds. Right: partners met per
participant, which is exactly their candidate-set size. Both panels: EDA §4 and
§6.](figures/fig1_structure.png){#fig-structure
width=94%}

The candidate set needs no construction and no negative sampling, which is unusual for an offline
recommender evaluation: **every one of the 551 participants met every opposite-sex participant
present in their wave** (verified in FE §4). Each candidate list is therefore fully observed, its
length being the number of partners met — 5 to 22, median 16 (@fig-structure). Because the lists are
short, a cut-off at rank 10 would cover most of a list, which is why the evaluation reports metrics
at rank 3 (@sec-protocol).

Two properties of the data limit what those metrics can show. A substantial minority of users have
no relevant item: 18.0% obtained no mutual match, leaving their reciprocal rank undefined, and 5.6%
accepted nobody; with a median of two matches per user, precision at rank 3 is capped at 2/3 for
half the sample, so methods must be compared against each other rather than against a theoretical
1.0 (EDA §10). The 21 folds are also not equivalent — per-wave match rates run from 8.3% to 31.0%, a
3.7-fold spread — so a mean across folds without its standard deviation would conceal more than it
reports. Part of that spread is by design: `condtn`, an experimental manipulation (limited versus
extensive choice), is constant within each wave and therefore perfectly confounded with the split
unit, explaining $R^2 \approx 0.11$ of the between-wave variance in match rate and correlating at
$+0.88$ with candidate-set size. Fold difficulty is thus partly structural, and `condtn` cannot
serve as a ranking feature, since a wave-constant value reorders nothing within a wave (EDA §10.1).

Attention is unequally distributed, which is what makes a popularity baseline non-trivial: the
size-free Gini coefficient of the acceptance rate is 0.323, the most desirable 10% of participants
absorb 22.8% of all acceptances, and 4.0% receive none (EDA §9; see @sec-baseline). The sample is
also demographically skewed — 55.2% of participants are European/Caucasian and the smallest racial
groups hold roughly 26 people (EDA §8) — so per-group fairness metrics would rest on cells too thin
to interpret, which is why @sec-analysis uses gender exposure as the fairness axis instead.

## Data hygiene

Missingness in the columns we rely on is minor: identifiers, decisions and the match label are
essentially complete, while 59 of the 195 columns are more than half empty, almost all of them the
follow-up surveys this project does not use (EDA §7). @tbl-hygiene lists the audits that did require
a decision.

| Finding | Evidence | Decision |
|:--------------------|:-------------------------|:-----------------------|
| Values outside documented ranges | 617 cells over 25 columns (0.23%); `gaming` reaches 14 on a 1–10 scale | Clip to the documented range before scaling; unclipped, one 14 stretches a min–max scaler across the column |
| Preference block on two scales | Documentation warns of a 1–10 scale in waves 6–9; that block proves already converted to shares, since only those waves hold non-integer values and they invert exactly to 1–10 answers | No rescaling required; normalise each participant's six weights to sum to one, since per-wave totals in fact range 90–148 |
| Sparse pre-date columns | `expnum` 77% missing, `mn_sat` 63%, `tuition` 58%, `income` 49%, and not missing at random | Exclude all four rather than impute half a column into a fairness analysis; keep `exphappy` (1.5%) |

: Data-quality findings and the decisions they produced; the three rows are established in EDA
§14.1, §12 and §7.1 respectively. {#tbl-hygiene}

One residual issue cannot be repaired and is reported rather than fixed. Waves 6–9 answered a
*different question*: participants rated each attribute from 1 to 10 instead of distributing 100
points across six attributes. Normalisation equalises the scale but not the question. Conversion
discards intensity — a participant answering 9 to all six becomes indistinguishable from one
answering 2 to all six — and the rating format elicits flatter profiles: on the identical normalised
scale, waves 6–9 profiles are 2.7 times less spread out, and none of those participants gave any
attribute zero weight against 20.2% elsewhere, because a minimum answer of 1 always leaves a positive
share. This affects 101 of 541 participants and 4 of the 21 folds (EDA §12.1).

## Feature set and leakage boundary {#sec-features}

### Where the boundary lies

Since the system must recommend pairings *before* the event, a feature is admissible only if it is
known at signup. Three independent sources place the boundary identically: our own problem statement
(@sec-intro), the project proposal, and the leakage note in the dataset documentation, which names
the admissible blocks explicitly (EDA §13). @tbl-leakage gives the resulting partition.

| Admissible (known at signup) | Excluded, and why |
|:----------------------------------|:---------------------------------|
| Signup profile: age, race, field, career, goal, going-out and dating frequency, importance of shared race and religion, expected happiness | Scorecard ratings `attr, sinc, intel, fun, amb, shar`, recorded *during* the date |
| 17 interest ratings, and `int_corr`, the pair's interest correlation | `like` and `prob`: near-restatements of the decision ($r = 0.51$, $0.31$) |
| Stated preference weights and their partner-side copies `pf_o_*` | The partner's in-date ratings `attr_o … prob_o`, `like_o`, `met_o` |
| Self-ratings `attr3_1 … amb3_1`; pair-level `samerace` | `dec_o` as an input: it is the reverse direction's *label* |
| Partner attributes joined on `pid` | `_s`, `_2`, `_3` surveys, recorded after the decisions; `condtn`; the four sparse columns of @tbl-hygiene |

: The pre-date feature boundary. The exclusion list is enforced programmatically in `sd_features.py`
and the check is executed in FE §10. {#tbl-leakage}

![Absolute correlation with the decision, on one axis: the in-date scorecard against the eight
strongest pre-date pair features. The remaining pre-date features are weaker
still. Correlations from EDA §11 and §13.2, and FE §9.](figures/fig2_leakage.png){#fig-leakage
width=88%}

Obeying the constraint is expensive, and @fig-leakage states the cost plainly: the signals that
dominate the decision are exactly the inadmissible ones — `like` at $|r| = 0.51$, attractiveness at
$0.49$, fun at $0.41$ — while the strongest admissible pair feature reaches $0.067$. The pre-date
task is not a weakened version of the in-date task but a substantially harder one, and comparisons
against published figures that use in-date ratings would be misleading.

A second consequence is stronger. Because participants attend exactly one wave, holding out a wave
removes those people entirely: across all 21 folds, **zero of 551 held-out participants and zero of
their partners have any training history** (EDA §15, per fold in FE §11). Every
fold is a complete cold start. Reputation features — how often a person accepts, how often they are
accepted — are the strongest pre-date signals available ($|r| \approx 0.40$ and $0.36$ estimated
leave-one-out, EDA §13.3), yet under this protocol they collapse to a constant on every test row,
and a constant cannot reorder a ranked list. They are therefore excluded by decision rather than
oversight, and the same fact re-specifies the baseline (@sec-baseline).

### The engineered feature set

The feature table holds 8,368 directed encounters described by 95 features in six blocks
(@tbl-features), plus identifiers and both labels. Partner attributes are attached by a map-join on
`pid`; we verified that the ready-made `pf_o_*` block is identical to the partner's own stated
preferences before relying on either (FE §4 and §6).

| Block | № | Example and rationale |
|:------------------|----:|:---------------------------------------------|
| Profile, both sides | 20 | `age`, `goal`, `go_out`: the demographic basis of a content model |
| Stated preferences | 12 | `pref_attr`: what each side says it wants, as shares summing to one |
| Self-ratings | 10 | `selfrate_attr`: the pre-date stand-in for what a person is like |
| Interests | 34 | `hiking`, `museums`: signup interest profiles for both sides |
| Dyadic comparisons | 12 | `age_diff`, `samerace`, `race_importance`, `int_corr` |
| Compatibility | 6 | `compat_a2b`, `compat_b2a`, `compat_harmonic` |

: The 95 engineered features, built in FE §5–§9; full definitions are in the exported data
dictionary. {#tbl-features}

The compatibility block carries the reciprocal idea. The natural formulation — the distance between
one person's stated preferences and the attribute ratings their partner received — is unavailable
here, since those ratings are in-date and, for a cold-start partner, absent from training
altogether. We substitute the partner's **self-ratings**, collected at signup and present for 98.4%
of participants across all 21 waves, and score each direction separately: `compat_a2b` applies the
decider's preference weights to the partner's self-rated attributes, `compat_b2a` is the mirror
image, and `compat_harmonic` is their harmonic mean, a single symmetric score (EDA §15.4,
built in FE §9).

![Stated preference weights against the weights implied by participants' actual decisions, by gender;
both normalised to sum to one. Source: EDA §12.](figures/fig3_stated_revealed.png){#fig-stated-revealed width=94%}

Two results justify the construction. Stated and revealed preferences genuinely diverge, and diverge
differently by gender (@fig-stated-revealed): both groups act on shared interests and fun
considerably more than they claim to, and on sincerity and intelligence considerably less. Were the
two aligned, a compatibility feature would add nothing beyond the attributes themselves. The two
directions also behave as correctly oriented directional features must: `compat_a2b`, which asks
whether the partner matches *the decider's* criteria, correlates $+0.067$ with the decider's own
decision, whereas its mirror `compat_b2a` does not ($-0.023$); against the symmetric `match` label
the two are equal, at $+0.037$ each (FE §9). Had the join been inverted, these signs would have
reversed.

### Leakage discipline in preprocessing

Preprocessing separates two kinds of operation. Clipping and min–max scaling use the *documented*
ranges from the data key rather than observed extrema, so they learn nothing from the data and
cannot leak, and a value means the same thing in every fold. Everything estimated — standardisation,
median imputation — is fitted on the training waves alone and applied to the held-out wave, because
a scaler fitted on the full table has already seen the fold it will be evaluated on. Categorical
codes are one-hot encoded against fixed category lists from the documentation, so the design matrix
keeps identical width across all 21 folds even when a fold contains no instance of a category. The
exported table is consequently unscaled by design, with the transformation applied inside the
cross-validation loop (FE §12; ranges audited in EDA §14).

# Baseline {#sec-baseline}

The baseline is a **popularity ranking**: candidates are ordered by desirability, the rate at which
they are accepted, ignoring who is choosing. It is a meaningful rather than a trivial reference
precisely because attention is concentrated — a size-free Gini of 0.323, the top decile absorbing
22.8% of acceptances (EDA §9) — so a ranker that merely learns who is popular already captures a
real regularity that a personalised method must beat.

The exploratory analysis established that it cannot be computed as usually worded (EDA §15.1):
ranking by "acceptances received" presumes a history, and under leave-one-wave-out no held-out
participant has one. Of the three available resolutions, computing desirability *within* the test
wave uses the labels being predicted and is admissible only if declared as a deliberately
optimistic, transductive upper bound, while scoring all candidates identically is leakage-free but
reduces the baseline to a random shuffle. We therefore adopt **predicted desirability**: a model
trained on the training waves that predicts a participant's acceptance rate from their signup
profile alone, then applied to unseen participants. This preserves what a popularity baseline is
meant to be — global, non-personalised, independent of who is choosing — while remaining computable
for a cold start. The training-side desirability the model is fitted against is not a raw
acceptance rate but a **Wilson lower bound** on it: the acceptance rate we can be confident a
participant is achieving *at least*, given how many dates that estimate rests on. The interval
shrinks a rate toward 0.5 when it comes from few observations and barely moves it when it comes
from many, so a participant accepted by 4 of 4 partners is scored 0.51 rather than 1.00, while one
accepted by 40 of 50 is scored 0.67 rather than 0.80 -- much closer to its raw value, since 50
dates is enough evidence to largely trust it. This is what keeps a small, lucky sample from
outranking a larger, more reliable one.
